newsitem.title: CHILE: FEATURE-Chile's southern tip attracts world's hardiest.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE-Chile's southern tip attracts world's hardiest.

text.p: They come in sailboats and tiny planes, riding bicycles or motorbikes, in wheelchairs or on foot.

Whatever kind of round-the-world adventure or endurance feat they are engaged in, most of them come through Punta Arenas. And this windy, isolated city at the southern tip of the Americas is more than happy to receive them.

Built on a hillside overlooking the Straits of Magellan, Punta Arenas has become something of a world capital of adventure tourism thanks to a steady flow of trekkers and thrill-seekers, including round-the-world sailors who must pass by unless they opt for the Panama Canal.

A growing number of people on their way to Antarctica add to the flow, as do Andean hikers and Alaska-to-Tierra del Fuego travelers who come to Punta Arenas to hop the ferry over to the giant island visible across the straits from the city.

"At this time of year we get a lot of bicyclists and motorbikers coming through. And solo yachtsmen too, though sometimes they come into town because they've been shipwrecked," Manuel Gonzalez, editor of the local newspaper Prensa Austral, said.

Whether they are hardy expeditionaries pushing the outer limits of human endurance, or mid-life crisis types looking for a new adventure, or merely people who want an unusual vacation, Punta Arenas has them all.

People passing through recently included a California couple motorcycling from one end of the Americas to the other for their honeymoon, an elderly Peruvian trying the same feat on a bicycle, various round-the-globe sailors and a Brazilian couple flying their single-engine plane around the world.

No fewer than 10 people, including famous British adventurer Sir Ranulph Fiennes, came through in the past few months on their way to Antarctica to try to walk across the frozen continent. One of them did it, Norway's Borge Ousland.

There was also a group attempting to row from South America to Antarctica, an American hoping to walk the full length of the Americas and a handicapped man who left Punta Arenas in a wheelchair saying he was bound for the United States. No one here knows if he made it.

"Being the first to do something like walking across the Antarctic gives people a feeling of satisfaction, of self-fulfilment. I guess that's why people do these things, for the challenge of it," said Lesley McGhee, who runs the local offices of British adventure tourism firm Adventure Network.

It also gives satisfaction to local businesses, who have seen tourism revive the city's economy after a history of booms and busts. Punta Arenas made its fortune in wool late in the last century and the grand mansions of the old wool barons still line the city's avenues, some of them now converted into offices or hotels and others crumbling in the cool drizzle.
FAR AWAY PANAMA CANAL HURT BUSINESS

The Panama Canal killed off the city's once-thriving international shipping trade early in this century and plunged it into an isolation from which it never emerged -- until tourism went big-time in the 1980s.

Now tour boats bound for Antarctica or the southern Chilean fjords clutter the harbour, new hotels have opened and the bustle of tourists gives Punta Arenas a certain swing and sophistication unique in Chile.

"We are like an island, in a way. So distant and remote, really at the end of the world, and I think that's what makes us so receptive to foreigners. We're so happy to see people coming again," Gonzalez said.

Locals fondly remember some of the colourful characters who have come through, like U.S. adventurer Norman Vaughan who trained for his climb up a mountain in Antarctica by running up and down the stairs of the eight-story hotel where he was staying, over and over again, at the age of 87.

The city's greatest adventurer of them all was, of course, Ferdinand Magellan, who sailed past in 1521 in his bid to become the first person to sail around the world. He was killed in the Phillipines but his crew completed the feat, arriving in Spain the next year, and a massive bronze statue of the explorer now stands in Punta Arenas' main square, gazing out at the straits named after him.
